```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(scales)
source(here("R", "theme_cours.R"))
```

Six sessions to learn R from scratch, for **Master GPE** students (development economics). **No prerequisites**: you start by installing R and finish with a reproducible report built on World Bank data.

## Where we are going

> **Common thread: growth, health and inequality, what does the data say about developing countries?**

```{=html}
<ol class="chain" aria-label="The course as a chain of six sessions"><li><span>R and RStudio</span></li><li><span>Import</span></li><li><span>Manipulate</span></li><li><span>Describe</span></li><li><span>Visualise</span></li><li><span>Report</span></li></ol>
```

**Import** data, **manipulate** it, **describe** it, **visualise** it, then **report** it: each session adds one link to the chain.

By Session 5 you will produce charts like this one: **richer countries live longer, but the gain flattens out** (the "Preston curve"). Every point is a country; the area shows its population.

```{r}
#| label: hero-preston
#| fig-alt: "Bubble chart of life expectancy against GDP per capita (log scale) for countries in 2019, coloured by region, bubble area proportional to population. Life expectancy rises with income, with diminishing gains at higher incomes."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code (you will write this in Session 5)"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.5
wdi <- read_csv(here("data", "wdi_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
# CAF life expectancy is unreliable in this WDI release (14.7 in 2009, 18.8 in 2022): exclude every year
wdi <- wdi |> mutate(life_exp = if_else(iso3c == "CAF", NA_real_, life_exp))

wdi |>
  filter(year == 2019, !is.na(gdp_pc_ppp), !is.na(life_exp), !is.na(region)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = gdp_pc_ppp, y = life_exp, size = population, colour = region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = label_dollar(scale_cut = cut_short_scale())) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 12, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pal_regions, labels = label_wrap(25)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 3, override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  labs(
    title = "Richer countries live longer, with diminishing returns",
    x = "GDP per capita (constant 2021 PPP $, log scale)",
    y = "Life expectancy at birth (years)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (WDI), 2019. Bubble area = population."
  )
```

## Before the first session

::: {.callout-important}
## To do at home

1. Install **R**: <https://cran.r-project.org/>.
2. Install **RStudio Desktop**: <https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/> (after R).
3. In RStudio: *File > New Project > New Directory* and create a project folder named `r-course`.
4. Download **[data.zip](data.zip)** and unzip it **into the `r-course` folder**, so that `data/` and `R/theme_cours.R` sit next to the `.Rproj` file (`here::here()` relies on this).
5. Install the packages: paste the block below in the RStudio **Console** and run it **once**. It takes a few minutes.
:::

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "janitor", "readxl", "writexl",
                   "lubridate", "scales", "WDI", "gt", "fixest",
                   "modelsummary", "ggrepel", "sf", "rnaturalearth",
                   "rnaturalearthdata", "patchwork", "plotly", "crosstalk",
                   "shiny"))
```

Expected folder tree:

```
r-course/
├── r-course.Rproj
├── data/
│   ├── wdi_panel.csv
│   ├── ...
│   └── raw/
└── R/
    └── theme_cours.R
```

## How to use this site

- Every session follows the same plan: objectives, explanations with code, **exercises**, then "Key takeaways".
- Type the code yourself in RStudio rather than copying it: that is how you learn.
- **Solutions are collapsed**: try first, then open to compare.
- An error is not a failure: read the message, it almost always says what is wrong.

## AI and code

AI assistants can explain an error message or an unfamiliar function. They must not replace your learning. **Always run the suggested code and understand every line** before using it: code that runs is not necessarily correct.
